title: News Feed
subtitle: Social feed architecture: hybrid fan-out, celebrity hot-key handling, and cursor pagination.
keyTakeaways: Use a hybrid fan-out model: push (fanout-on-write) post IDs into timelines for normal users (< 25,000 followers), and pull (fanout-on-read) dynamically at query time for high-follower celebrity accounts.
Store only lightweight references (postId, authorId, createdAt) in user timeline caches, hydrating post text and author metadata in bulk using multi-get queries against a cached object store.
Always use cursor-based pagination (based on post timestamp or Snowflake ID) instead of SQL OFFSET/LIMIT so scrolling remains stable and duplicate-free as new posts arrive.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A News Feed system aggregates, ranks, and serves a personalized stream of content posted by friends and followed entities with sub-second response times.
bullets: Functional: Users can publish posts (text, image URLs); users can follow/unfollow other users; users can view a chronological or ranked feed of posts from people they follow.
Functional: Fast pagination support as users scroll down their feed.
Non-Functional: Sub-200ms feed generation latency (p99); eventual consistency for post delivery (within 5 seconds across followers).
Non-Functional: High availability on read operations (feed browsing must remain operational even during database write degradations).
Out of Scope: Full-text post search, ad delivery auction engines, and live video streaming feeds.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: News feed platforms exhibit severe read skew and extreme follower variance between ordinary users and celebrity accounts.
bullets: User Base: 300 million daily active users (DAU). Each user checks their feed 5 times per day = 1.5 billion feed views/day (~17,500 reads/second average, peaking at 40,000 RPS).
Write Volume: 50 million new posts created per day (~600 writes/second average, peaking at 2,500 writes/second).
Follower Distribution: Median user has 200 followers; celebrity accounts have 10 to 50 million followers.

Timeline Cache Sizing: Store the latest 800 post IDs per active user. 800 post IDs * 24 bytes (post_id, author_id, timestamp) = ~19.2 KB per user. For 300 million DAU, timeline cache requires ~5.7 TB of RAM across a Redis cluster.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Analyzing fan-out write amplification proves why pure fanout-on-write collapses when celebrities post.
bullets: Pure fanout-on-write write amplification: If a celebrity with 30 million followers posts, writing to 30 million user timelines generates 30 million cache writes for a single post. At 100 celebrity posts per day, this creates billions of background writes, saturating message queues and Redis clusters.
Cache memory budget: 300 million DAU * 800 items * 24 bytes = 5.76 TB. Divided across 64 Redis nodes (96 GB RAM each), each node comfortably holds ~90 GB of timeline data.
Post content storage: 50 million posts/day * 1 KB average text/metadata = 50 GB/day = 18.2 TB/year in persistent storage (PostgreSQL/Cassandra).

codeSnippet.title: News Feed Capacity & Memory Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
NEWS FEED CAPACITY ESTIMATION WORKSHEET (300M DAU / 600M POSTS PER DAY)
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT (QPS)
   - Avg Post Write QPS       : 600,000,000 / 86,400        = 6,944 QPS
   - Peak Post Write QPS (3x) : 6,944 * 3                   = 20,832 QPS
   - Avg Timeline Read QPS    : 6,000,000,000 / 86,400      = 69,444 QPS
   - Peak Timeline Read QPS   : 69,444 * 3                  = 208,332 QPS
   - Internal Fanout ZADD QPS : ~7,000 * 150 (non-celeb)    = 1,050,000 ops/sec

2. REDIS MEMORY (TIMELINE ZSET + POST HYDRATION CACHE)
   - Timeline Entry Size      : 8B(postId) + 8B(authorId) + 8B(score) + 16B(ZSET) = 40 B
   - Per-User Timeline Cap    : 800 posts * 40 B            = 32 KB / user
   - 500M Active Users Cache  : 500,000,000 * 32 KB         = 16.0 TB (Primary)
   - With 1 Replica (HA)      : 16.0 TB * 2                 = 32.0 TB Total Redis RAM
   - Hot Post Metadata Cache  : 360M hot posts * 1 KB       = 360 GB RAM

3. 5-YEAR DISK STORAGE (POSTS + SOCIAL GRAPH)
   - Daily Post Volume        : 600M * 1 KB                 = 600 GB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Post Storage  : 600 GB * 365 * 5            = 1.095 PB
   - 3x Replicated + Overhead : 1.095 PB * 3 * 1.3          = 4.27 PB
   - Social Graph (1B * 200)  : 200B edges * 24 B * 3 (rep) = 14.4 TB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Ingress (Writes)    : 20,832 QPS * 1 KB           = 20.8 MB/s  (166 Mbps)
   - Peak Egress (Reads)      : 208,332 QPS * 20 KB (page)  = 4.16 GB/s  (33.3 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Feed APIs must be paginated via cursors to avoid duplicate or skipped posts when new items arrive while a user is scrolling.
bullets: Read API: `GET /v1/feed?cursor=1727788800123&limit=20` returns `{ items: [...], nextCursor: "1727788795000" }`.
Write API: `POST /v1/posts` takes `{ content, mediaUrls[] }` and returns `{ postId, createdAt }`.
Timeline data model: Stored in Redis Sorted Sets (`ZSET`), where the key is `timeline:{userId}`, the score is the post creation timestamp, and the value is `postId`.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture cleanly separates post publishing, background timeline fan-out workers, and the feed assembly read pipeline.
bullets: Post Service: Persists post metadata to Cassandra/Postgres, pushes creation events to Kafka, and notifies the Fan-out Service.
Fan-Out Worker Cluster: Consumes post events, queries the Follower Service, and injects post IDs into Redis timelines for regular users.

Feed Assembly Service: Handles feed queries. Fetches the user's timeline from Redis, queries celebrity posts via fanout-on-read, merges and ranks candidates, and hydrates full post objects from cache.
Metadata Hydration Layer: Uses multi-get calls against Memcached/Redis to hydrate author profiles and post text in a single network round trip.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: The hybrid fan-out model combines the strengths of push and pull strategies while neutralizing their respective failure modes.
bullets: Fan-out on write (Push) for regular users: When a user with 200 followers posts, the fan-out worker inserts the `postId` into all 200 followers' Redis Sorted Sets within 100ms. When those followers open their feed, reading is an instant O(1) Redis call.

Fan-out on read (Pull) for celebrities: When an account with >25,000 followers posts, the fan-out worker does NOT write to follower timelines. Instead, the post is saved only to the celebrity's author timeline.

Feed merge at read time: When a user requests their feed, the Feed Service fetches their Redis push timeline and pulls the latest posts from all followed celebrities, merging the streams using a k-way heap sort before applying ranking scores.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Scaling feed systems requires handling inactive users, cache evictions, and database partitions cleanly.
bullets: Inactive user pruning: Only maintain pre-computed push timelines for users who have logged in within the past 14 days. When an inactive user logs in, trigger an asynchronous rebuild of their timeline from database records.

Cursor stability vs OFFSET: Never use SQL `OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20`. If 5 new posts are published while the user is reading page 1, scrolling to page 2 with OFFSET will repeat 5 posts the user just saw. Cursors (`WHERE created_at < cursor LIMIT 20`) guarantee stable pagination.

Circuit breaking celebrity services: If the follower graph or celebrity feed puller experiences elevated latency, serve the user's pre-computed push timeline immediately with a degraded banner rather than timing out the entire feed.

tradeOffs.option: Hybrid Fan-Out (Push for regular, Pull for celebrities)
tradeOffs.pros: Sub-100ms read latency for 95% of users; prevents celebrity write amplification storms from crushing Redis.
tradeOffs.cons: More complex read path; requires k-way merge sorting at query time for followed celebrity accounts.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large-scale social networks (Twitter/X, Instagram, LinkedIn) with skewed follower distributions.

tradeOffs.pros: Ultra-fast read path: generating a feed is a single Redis ZREVRANGEBYSCORE call.
tradeOffs.cons: Catastrophic write amplification when high-follower accounts post; consumes massive queue bandwidth and memory.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Enterprise collaboration tools (Slack, Teams) where group sizes are bounded (e.g., < 1,000 members).

tradeOffs.pros: Zero write amplification; post publishing is instantaneous; storage footprint is minimal.
tradeOffs.cons: Slow read path: every feed view requires querying hundreds of followed users and sorting results in real time.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-traffic platforms or systems where users follow very few accounts.

interviewTip: When an interviewer asks how your feed handles a celebrity with 50 million followers, explain why pure push fails (write amplification) and propose the hybrid model: push for regular users, pull on read for celebrities, and merge results at query time.
